The Road Ahead — Extensions, Ecosystems, and the Browser

Source: vignettes/future-extensions.Rmd
future-extensions.Rmd

Why a “road ahead” vignette?

aRtifacts ships today as a deliberately small engine: snapshots, diffs, and rules. That minimalism is a feature, not a limitation — it means the core never needs to know what your data means, only what makes each row unique and what properties it should satisfy.

Everything domain-specific — be it clinical, financial, manufacturing, or genomic — belongs in extension modules that talk the language of that world while relying on the same deterministic engine underneath.

This vignette paints the picture of where that idea leads.

1 — Therapeutic-area extensions

The bundled SDTM and ADaM checks are a proof of concept, not the ceiling. Imagine companion packages tuned to an entire therapeutic area:

Extension Focus Example rules
aRtifacts.oncology RECIST, tumor assessments Best overall response derivation, target-lesion completeness per visit
aRtifacts.vaccines Immunogenicity, reactogenicity Seroconversion flag consistency, grading-scale alignment with FDA toxicity tables
aRtifacts.cardio ECG, vital-sign trending QTc derivation checks, Bazett vs. Fridericia concordance
aRtifacts.neuro Cognitive-scale scoring ADAS-Cog item-to-total reconciliation, MMSE floor/ceiling detection
aRtifacts.RWE Claims, EHR, registries ICD-10 code validity, enrollment-gap detection, index-date anchoring

Each extension is just a collection of CoreRule objects and optional convenience checkers — exactly the same pattern used by check_adsl() and check_bds() today. Because CoreRule is an S7 class with a pure-function evaluator, packaging new rules is as simple as writing functions that return TRUE / FALSE per row or per domain.

For contributors: Writing a therapeutic-area module requires zero knowledge of the diff engine. You define rules; the engine runs them.

2 — Risk-Based Quality Management (RBQM)

Regulatory guidance (ICH E6 R2, and more recently R3) emphasizes risk-proportionate approaches to data quality. aRtifacts’ architecture maps naturally onto an RBQM workflow:

Severity tiers

A CoreRule can carry a severity property — "critical", "major", "minor" — allowing organizations to classify risks centrally and filter downstream reporting.

high_risk <- new_rule(
  id = "RBQM-001",
  title = "Subject missing informed-consent date",
  topology = "A1",
  scope = "record",
  intent = "clinical_review",
  domain = "DM",
  severity = "critical",
  fn = function(data, context, rule) data[is.na(data[["RFICDTC"]]), , drop = FALSE]
)

Longitudinal risk scoring

Because you can compare run_rules() outputs between two builds and track which flags appeared, disappeared, or persisted, you get a ready-made time-series of risk signals per domain, per site, per study:

Build 12   →   Build 13
 critical: 3        critical: 1   ← 2 resolved
 major: 17          major: 19     ← 2 new, trend watch

A downstream dashboard can consume this flag-state delta output directly — no ETL step required.

Key Risk Indicators (KRIs)

run_rules() output is a tidy data frame. Aggregating flag counts by site, country, or study yields KRIs that feed directly into RBQM central-monitoring displays:

ctx <- new_rule_context(current = snapshot)
flags <- run_rules(ctx, rules)
kri   <- aggregate(flag ~ site, data = flags, FUN = length)

The takeaway: aRtifacts doesn’t replace your RBQM platform — it gives your RBQM platform a deterministic, version-controlled data feed with zero manual curation.

3 — Organization-specific terminology and style

Every organization has its own naming conventions, controlled terminology, and review expectations. The engine is deliberately silent about these — but extension modules can enforce them rigorously:

Custom terminology dictionaries 

# Hypothetical aRtifacts.myorg module
org_terms <- list(
  RACE = c("WHITE", "BLACK OR AFRICAN AMERICAN",
           "ASIAN", "AMERICAN INDIAN OR ALASKA NATIVE",
           "NATIVE HAWAIIAN OR OTHER PACIFIC ISLANDER",
           "MULTIPLE", "NOT REPORTED", "UNKNOWN"),
  SEX  = c("M", "F", "U", "UNDIFFERENTIATED")
)

term_rules <- lapply(names(org_terms), function(var) {
  allowed <- org_terms[[var]]
  new_rule(
    id = paste0("TERM-", var),
    title = paste(var, "must be in org codelist"),
    topology = "A1",
    scope = "record",
    intent = "data_entry",
    domain = "DM",
    fn = function(data, context, rule) data[!(data[[var]] %in% allowed), , drop = FALSE]
  )
})

Variable-naming conventions 

 naming_rule <- new_rule(
  id = "STYLE-001",
  title = "All variables must be uppercase, 8 chars max",
  topology = "A1",
  scope = "record",
  intent = "programming_etl",
  domain = "DM",
  fn = function(data, context, rule) {
    nms <- names(data)
    if (all(nms == toupper(nms)) && all(nchar(nms) <= 8)) return(data.frame())
    data[seq_len(min(1L, nrow(data))), , drop = FALSE]
  }
)

Metadata-driven rule generation

For organizations that maintain a metadata repository (define.xml, a spec database, an internal data dictionary), rules can be generated programmatically from that repository — one CoreRule per variable, type-check, codelist, or cross-domain relationship:

# Pseudocode: generate rules from a define.xml parse
for (var_def in parse_define_xml("define2-0-0.xml")) {
  rule <- new_rule(
    id = paste0("DEF-", var_def$OID),
    title = paste(var_def$Name, "codelist check"),
    topology = "A1",
    scope = "record",
    intent = "data_entry",
    domain = "DM",
    fn = make_codelist_rule_fn(var_def$CodeList)
  )
}

The pattern: Your metadata is the single source of truth. aRtifacts turns it into executable checks — no copy-paste, no drift.

4 — Beyond clinical: other industries

Because the engine knows nothing about clinical trials, it works anywhere you have keyed tabular data and care about quality over time:

  • Finance / Accounting — Reconcile GL snapshots across periods; flag journal entries that violate segregation-of-duties rules.
  • Manufacturing / IoT — Snapshot sensor readings by batch + timestamp; diff successive batches to catch drift.
  • Genomics / Bioinformatics — Snapshot variant-call tables; flag unexpected allele-frequency shifts between pipeline runs.
  • Survey / Social science — Track questionnaire data across collection waves; detect impossible transitions (e.g., age decreasing).

The companion-package pattern is identical: define CoreRule objects that speak the language of your domain, and the core engine handles the rest.

5 — Running in the browser with R-WASM

One of the most exciting developments in the R ecosystem is webR — a build of R that compiles to WebAssembly and runs entirely in the browser, no server required.

aRtifacts is a natural fit for R-WASM because of three deliberate design choices:

Minimal dependency footprint

aRtifacts imports exactly one package: S7. S7 is a pure-R package with no compiled code. That means the entire aRtifacts + S7 stack can be loaded in a webR session with no native compilation step — just install and go.

// JavaScript — loading aRtifacts inside a webR session
const webR = new WebR();
await webR.init();
await webR.installPackages(['S7', 'aRtifacts']);
await webR.evalR('library(aRtifacts)');

Pure-function architecture

Every function in aRtifacts is referentially transparent: same inputs, same outputs, no side effects, no file-system access, no database connections. That is exactly the execution model WebAssembly enforces — making aRtifacts one of the most WASM-friendly R packages by design.

What this unlocks

Scenario How it works
Client-side data review A reviewer opens a static HTML app, drops two CSVs, and instantly sees a diff — nothing leaves their laptop.
Shinylive dashboards A Shinylive app (Shiny for R in WASM) embeds aRtifacts for interactive snapshot comparison, rule execution, and flag trending — deployed as a static site on GitHub Pages or SharePoint.
Offline / air-gapped environments Validated environments with no internet access can bundle a WASM build; auditors run checks on-site without installing R.
Training and education Interactive tutorials (e.g., via learnr / webR-powered quarto docs) let learners experiment with snapshots and rules in the browser.
Embedded review widgets A <webr-widget> tag in a Quarto document lets readers re-run aRtifacts code cells live, turning static reports into interactive notebooks.

A glimpse: Shinylive + aRtifacts 

# This Shiny app can be deployed as a Shinylive static site
library(shiny)
library(aRtifacts)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("aRtifacts — Browser-Native Data Diff"),
  fileInput("file_v1", "Upload baseline CSV"),
  fileInput("file_v2", "Upload updated CSV"),
  textInput("keys", "Key columns (comma-separated)", value = "USUBJID"),
  actionButton("go", "Compare"),
  tableOutput("diff_out")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  observeEvent(input$go, {
    keys <- trimws(strsplit(input$keys, ",")[[1]])
    v1 <- new_domain_snapshot("data", read.csv(input$file_v1$datapath),
                              key_vars = keys, build_id = "v1")
    v2 <- new_domain_snapshot("data", read.csv(input$file_v2$datapath),
                              key_vars = keys, build_id = "v2")
    output$diff_out <- renderTable(diff_values(v1, v2))
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

Zero infrastructure, zero servers, zero install.
A static HTML file, a browser, and the full power of aRtifacts.

6 — The ecosystem vision

Putting it all together, the long-term picture looks like this:

                    ┌───────────────────────────┐
                    │     aRtifacts  (core)      │
                    │  snapshots · diffs · rules  │
                    └─────────────┬───────────────┘
                                  │
              ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
              │                   │                    │
     ┌────────▼────────┐ ┌───────▼────────┐ ┌────────▼────────┐
     │ aRtifacts.sdtm  │ │ aRtifacts.adam │ │ aRtifacts.myorg │
     │  SDTM rules +   │ │  ADaM rules + │ │  org terminology │
     │  tabulation QC   │ │  BDS / ADSL   │ │  + style rules   │
     └────────┬─────────┘ └───────┬────────┘ └────────┬────────┘
              │                   │                    │
              ▼                   ▼                    ▼
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │        Therapeutic-area & industry extensions            │
     │  .oncology · .vaccines · .cardio · .finance · .genomics │
     └─────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                               │
              ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
              │                │                 │
        ┌─────▼─────┐  ┌──────▼──────┐  ┌───────▼───────┐
        │  Desktop R │  │  Shinylive  │  │  webR widget  │
        │  (server)  │  │  (browser)  │  │  (embedded)   │
        └────────────┘  └─────────────┘  └───────────────┘

Every box in this diagram shares the same DomainSnapshot → CoreRule → run_rules() → flag-state comparison pipeline. The only difference is which rules you load and where R runs.

Getting involved

aRtifacts is open source and contribution-friendly. Whether you want to:

  • Add rules for a therapeutic area you know well,
  • Build an org module that encodes your company’s standards,
  • Create a Shinylive demo that showcases browser-native data review, or
  • Improve the core with better diff algorithms or richer metadata,

the architecture is designed to make your contribution self-contained and composable.

Start small: write one new_rule() constructor, wrap it in a test, submit a PR. That’s the atomic unit of contribution — and it’s all you need to make the ecosystem a little better.

Happy building.
